subject: Business Models
title: All-You-Can-Eat Pricing
description: A micro-lesson that makes All-You-Can-Eat Pricing usable.

hook.text: Buffet restaurants charge one price. Heavy eaters and light eaters pay the same.

buildup.text: ClassPass offers unlimited fitness classes for one monthly fee. Same principle: flat rate, variable use.

discovery.text: These models profit because most subscribers overestimate their usage. Gym memberships prove this daily.

twist.text: Netflix uses this too. Power users watch 8 hours/day but pay the same as someone who watches once a month.

climax.text: All-you-can-eat pricing works when average consumption is far below maximum capacity.

punchline.text: Unlimited access, limited use. Flat pricing profits from hope.

details.summary: All-you-can-eat pricing charges a single flat fee for unlimited access to a product or service. Netflix offers unlimited streaming for one monthly price. Gym memberships, software site licenses, and unlimited data plans all use this model to simplify purchasing decisions.
details.whyItMatters: Flat-rate unlimited pricing appeals to customers who fear unpredictable bills and value simplicity. Providers profit because most users consume far less than the theoretical maximum, making average revenue per user higher than average cost per user.
takeaways: Single flat fee covers unlimited product or service usage
Providers profit because most customers underuse their entitlement
Simplicity and predictability drive strong customer preference

faq.question: Why do all-you-can-eat models work financially for providers?
faq.answer: The flat fee is set above average usage cost but below the cost of maximum possible usage. Most customers consume moderately, paying more than their usage costs. Heavy users are subsidized by light users. The predictability also reduces billing complexity and customer support costs.

faq.question: When do all-you-can-eat pricing models fail?
faq.answer: When power users consume disproportionately expensive resources, when marginal costs per unit are high, or when the pricing attracts only heavy users while light users choose cheaper alternatives. Mobile carriers abandoned truly unlimited data plans after heavy users overwhelmed networks.
